stories.headline: Nvidia board prepares to oust CEO, name interim chief
stories.claim: Nvidia's board reportedly prepares to oust CEO Jensen Huang after a second extramarital affair, with CFO Colette Kress possibly named interim chief.
stories.summary: Semafor, citing people familiar with the matter, reports that Nvidia's board is preparing to remove founder and CEO Jensen Huang, possibly as soon as Wednesday, after media reports of a second extramarital affair. Some directors reportedly favour naming CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO, and an outside search firm has reportedly been hired. Bloomberg reports Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji is among those considered. Nvidia shares reportedly fell over 8% after hours, hitting a 52-week low. The board has also reportedly launched a Wachtell Lipton-led probe into whether Huang divulged corporate secrets, and two US senators asked the administration to preserve related documents.
key_points: Some Nvidia board members reportedly favour appointing CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO if Huang is ousted.
The full board had not decided and was scheduled to meet on Wednesday evening, per sources.
Nvidia reportedly hired an outside search firm; Johny Srouji is reportedly among candidates, per Bloomberg.
Shares reportedly fell more than 8% in after-hours trading, to a 52-week low.
Nvidia's board has launched a probe into whether Huang divulged corporate secrets or endangered US national security, linked to an affair with a suspected Chinese operative.
Senators Coons and Warren asked officials to preserve documents on Nvidia chip exports and the affair.
stories.likelihood_reason: Bloomberg is usually reliable, but the report cites a single anonymous person and Nvidia's board has so far only said it is investigating; the board's own denial of a security breach leaves the outcome open.

stories.headline: UK chip start-up Fractile hits $7bn valuation
stories.claim: UK AI chip start-up Fractile reportedly valued at $7bn after a $720m Series C round.
stories.summary: London-based AI chip start-up Fractile has reportedly been valued at $7bn, following a Series C funding round worth $720m. The figure is a sharp jump from the roughly $1bn valuation it reached in its May round, when it raised $220m. Reuters first reported the valuation, citing a person involved in the deal, and the founder and CEO Walter Goodwin confirmed the funding on X. Thrive Capital, Lightspeed, Redpoint and Founders Fund led the round, according to Goodwin. The UK's Sovereign AI Venture Fund and the British Business Bank also took part, framing the investment as a way to reduce reliance on overseas supply chains. Fractile is building inference hardware for agentic AI and was reported in August to have agreed a deal to sell about $250m of chips to Anthropic for 2027 deployment. The round underlines investor appetite for challengers to Nvidia in AI chips.
key_points: Fractile, founded in 2022 and based in London and Bristol, has reportedly reached a $7bn valuation.
The Series C round was worth $720m, up from $220m raised in May at around $1bn valuation.
Thrive Capital, Lightspeed, Redpoint and Founders Fund led the round, per CEO Walter Goodwin.
The UK Sovereign AI Venture Fund and British Business Bank also invested, citing sovereign capability goals.
Fractile aims to build fast inference hardware for agentic AI; an August report said it agreed to sell about $250m of chips to Anthropic for 2027.
The deal signals continued investor appetite for Nvidia challengers in AI hardware.
stories.market_take: Private valuation with no listed stock; may buoy sentiment for AI chip challengers.

stories.headline: Poundland owner extracted millions when chain was on ‘knife-edge’, MPs say
stories.claim: MPs accuse Poundland's owner Gordon Brothers of extracting millions while the chain was on a knife-edge, as Poundland seeks more legal protection.
stories.summary: Poundland's management is asking the High Court for a further two-week shelter from creditors, as the discount chain's owner Gordon Brothers faces criticism from MPs. The Commons business committee chair, Liam Byrne, said Gordon Brothers may have jeopardised thousands of jobs after it took millions out of the business over 17 months. Poundland employs 12,000 people across 600 UK and Irish stores and has only enough cash for a short period, although sales are reportedly up year on year. Gordon Brothers is in talks with three potential bidders and Martin Property Group, but reported bids are worth less than the £30m shareholder debt. Alix Partners is lined up as administrator if the protection lapses.
key_points: Poundland management will seek a further 10 working days of protection from creditors from the High Court.
Gordon Brothers, which bought the chain for £1 from Pepco in June 2025, has released £10m more to keep stock flowing.
Reported bids are understood to be below the £30m of shareholder debt, and Gordon Brothers may favour a break-up.
Martin Property Group's first bid was rejected, and Xyra Group is reported to have offered about £12m upfront.
Alix Partners is already lined up to act as administrators if the rescue fails.

stories.headline: Russia says it launched a massive overnight strike on Ukrainian military factories
stories.claim: Russia says it launched a massive overnight strike on Ukrainian military factories, including in Kyiv, as Ukraine's capital reported casualties.
stories.summary: Russia's military said it carried out a massive overnight strike on military factories across Ukraine, including a rocket factory in Kyiv. Kyiv's mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said a Russian drone hit a nine-storey apartment block in the Solomyanskyi district, killing one woman and injuring five people. Russia said Ukraine launched 71 drones across Russia overnight, with five heading for Moscow downed. The Russian Defence Ministry also said it hit electricity substations in the Zhytomyr region, and Rivne region reported damage to energy and civilian infrastructure. The report is a Reuters story republished across several outlets, with the figures coming from the two sides and local officials.

stories.headline: Google Home gets more reliable Gemini commands, faster timers, and Nest camera fixes
stories.claim: Google rolls out its first November Google Home update, fixing Gemini smart-home commands, timers, and Nest camera issues.
stories.summary: Google has issued its first November update for Google Home, aimed at making Gemini more reliable when controlling smart-home devices. Gemini should now handle complex commands with fewer refusals and ask follow-up questions when several devices match a request. Timers and alarms should respond faster, and broadcast messages should play more quickly. The update also fixes problems with first-generation Nest Cam, Nest Cam IQ and original wired Nest Doorbell models that had been migrated to Google Home. New features include one-press Eco mode across multiple Nest thermostats and Google Wallet home keys for compatible Aliro smart locks in Public Preview. Rollout is gradual and some features are limited to early-access or preview users.

stories.headline: Russia is already at war with Europe in space
stories.claim: Analysts say a space war between Russia and Europe, and Russia and Ukraine, is already under way, with satellites now central to the conflict.
stories.summary: Analysts quoted in The Times, Al Jazeera and DongA Science argue that the Russia-Ukraine war has already spread into space, with both sides trying to disrupt each other's satellite capabilities. Reports cite Ukraine's August strike on the Progress centre in Samara, which hit facilities including the Soyuz assembly site, and a Russian satellite approaching Ukraine's Iceye imaging satellite, which experts say was probably intimidation. Russia has reportedly used jamming, laser interference and close-approach satellites against foreign assets. Al Jazeera's piece places this within a wider debate on Europe's need to fund Ukraine and build a war economy, as Washington's support becomes less certain. The Times and Al Jazeera texts are partial, so the detail rests mainly on the DongA and Al Jazeera versions.
key_points: Experts say the militarisation of space is accelerating in the Russia-Ukraine war, with satellites central to military operations.

stories.headline: Global electric vehicle sales return to growth in October
stories.claim: Global EV and plug-in hybrid sales rose 8% in October to 2.09 million, returning to growth, per Benchmark data.
stories.summary: Global sales of battery-electric and plug-in hybrid cars rose 8% year on year to 2.09 million vehicles in October, ending a stretch of decline, according to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. Year-to-date volumes are up 5% at 17.5 million. Europe grew 36%, helped by subsidies, higher fuel prices and EU emissions rules, while China's domestic decline narrowed to 12% as makers pushed exports. Chinese passenger NEV exports hit a monthly record of almost 600,000 units. North America returned to growth with a 24% rise, but only because October was the first month measured against a period without the US federal EV tax credit, so the market has stabilised at a lower level rather than recovered.
key_points: Global plug-in and battery EV sales reached 2.09 million in October, up 8% on a year earlier.
Year-to-date global volumes are 17.5 million, up 5%.
European sales rose 36%, supported by subsidies, fuel prices and EU emissions legislation.
China's domestic decline narrowed to 12%, with passenger NEV exports close to 600,000, a monthly record.
US sales rose 24% against a weak base after the federal EV tax credit ended, and rest-of-world sales rose 85%.
stories.market_take: Strong European and export growth supports carmakers exposed to EVs, though China's domestic weakness remains a drag.

stories.headline: The Kremlin can hide the death toll. It can’t hide the graves.
stories.claim: Independent researchers and photographers are documenting Russia's war dead as the Kremlin hides casualty data and arrests people for photographing graves.
stories.summary: Russia is hiding the true cost of its war in Ukraine, and independent researchers are using gravestones and court records to expose losses far above official figures. Russia 200, a database run by Mediazona and the BBC's Russian service, lists nearly 283,000 named dead soldiers, while the UK Foreign Office and Dutch intelligence estimate more than half a million Russian losses. Russian courts have handed a 14-year sentence to a man who photographed soldiers' graves, and several dozen people have been arrested since the summer on treason charges. Moscow has halted official casualty data, including Rosstat's excess death figures, and restricted court cases declaring soldiers dead, which rose to about 90,000 in 2025. Analysts say the secrecy helps the Kremlin keep recruiting soldiers.
key_points: A Russian court sentenced a man in Yaroslavl to 14 years for photographing soldiers' gravestones in September.
Russia 200 lists almost 283,000 named dead soldiers, but the true toll is likely higher.

stories.headline: The AO3 Shutdown Is Pitting Fanfic Readers Against Authors
stories.claim: AO3's shutdown after a security incident has sparked fights over fanfic copies on mirror sites and Google Drive libraries.
stories.summary: The Archive of Our Own, the fan fiction site hosting more than 18.8 million works, has been offline since 29 October after a 'security incident', and its team says it could stay dark for up to four weeks. In the meantime, fans have copied stories onto mirror sites and shared Google Drive libraries, often without authors' permission. That has caused friction, with writers worried about security risks, privacy and AI scraping, while some readers have been accused of entitlement. A collaborative platform, Ellipsus, says sign-ups have risen more than 500 percent since the outage. The episode shows how fan fiction has moved into the mainstream, helped by shows such as Heated Rivalry.

stories.headline: Poland turns to home-grown giant for its defense buildup
stories.claim: Poland's state-owned PGZ is becoming the centrepiece of a rapid defence buildup, but faces fragmentation and political risk.
stories.summary: Poland is pouring money into its military, and state-owned Polish Armaments Group (PGZ) is at the heart of the buildup. Poland plans to spend 200 billion złoty (about €45.7 billion) on defence this year, 4.8 percent of GDP and the highest share in NATO. PGZ, formed in 2013 from about 50 companies, reported 18.4 billion złoty of revenue in 2025 and profit of 2.8 billion złoty. Most of its deals have been no-bid contracts, which a think tank has criticised. Poland also takes the largest share of the EU's €150 billion SAFE loans-for-arms programme, almost €44 billion. Political risk is growing, as a former prime minister has called for PGZ to be dissolved ahead of next year's election.
key_points: Poland plans to spend 200 billion złoty (€45.7 billion), or 4.8 percent of GDP, on defence in 2026, the highest level in NATO.

stories.summary: US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and his aides were rebuked by a sentinel at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington after some in the group were heard laughing following a Veterans Day ceremony. The guard loudly reminded the group to maintain silence and respect, and Hegseth looked back at him as he climbed the steps. The Pentagon said the soldier had correctly reminded everyone to keep decorum. Critics including former Republican congressman Adam Kinzinger condemned the behaviour. The incident follows a House vote of 211 to 204 that blocked an impeachment effort against Hegseth over his handling of the Iran war and other conflicts. Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress in the 3 November midterms, and Democrat Hakeem Jeffries is expected to become House speaker.

stories.headline: Investors worry the AI trade needs Nvidia's Huang and its largesse
stories.claim: Nvidia shares fell after reports of CEO Jensen Huang's affairs and a board review, raising fears for the AI trade.
stories.summary: Nvidia's shares fell about 8% after hours as investors worried that the chipmaker's board might oust chief executive Jensen Huang, a figure central to the AI boom. The board was meeting late on Wednesday to decide his fate after reports of two extramarital affairs, one involving a businesswoman alleged to be a Chinese spy. Nasdaq 100 futures dropped nearly 1% in Asia, and customers such as CoreWeave and Naver were hit, while AMD and Broadcom rose. Chinese GPU makers Moore Threads, MetaX and Cambricon jumped close to 10% on hopes of gaining market share. The bigger concern is that Nvidia, which has been financing its customers through equity stakes and other commitments, might scale back that funding under a new leader, potentially slowing the AI build-out. Nvidia's shares have risen roughly 900% since ChatGPT launched four years ago.

stories.headline: Democrat Scott Colom wins Senate race in Mississippi
stories.claim: Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi US Senate race, defeating incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith by under 5,000 votes.
stories.summary: Democrat Scott Colom has won the US Senate race in Mississippi, defeating Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith by fewer than 5,000 votes out of nearly a million counted. Colom took 49.2% of the vote to Hyde-Smith's 48.7%, with an independent taking 2.1%. He becomes the first Black senator from Mississippi in more than 140 years and ends a Republican winning streak in the state dating back to 1982. Hyde-Smith conceded in a video posted on X. The result came after a count that lasted from the 4 November election. Trump won the state by more than 22 points in 2024, so the race was far closer than expected. The Democrats will hold 55 seats in the 100-member Senate, with an Alaska race still to be called, and have also taken control of the House in the midterms.
key_points: Scott Colom, 43, won with 49.2% against 48.7% for incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith.

stories.headline: Study suggests not all obesity means ill-health
stories.claim: Nature study says only a quarter to a third of obese people have clinical obesity, proposing a BMI-plus diagnosis framework.
stories.summary: A new study published in Nature suggests that only about a quarter to a third of people diagnosed with obesity are genuinely in poor health. Analysing almost 850,000 adults from China, Britain, the US and Spain, the researchers estimate that 1% to 3% of people classed as obese by BMI alone would not be, while 5% to 9% more would be diagnosed once body fat is considered. The framework adds waist circumference and body fat to BMI, and checks for organ dysfunction such as heart or liver problems. Senior author Francesco Rubino of King's College London said BMI's inaccuracy is well known but no better system existed. The findings could change how obesity is diagnosed and treated, a WHO-estimated condition affecting over a billion people worldwide.

The IRGC blamed the tankers for ignoring warnings and using an unauthorised southern route, though it gave few details of the cause. Iranian state media said the vessels exploded after hitting naval mines, and the IRGC has made several similar claims in recent weeks. Since the Middle East war began in late February, Tehran has restricted traffic through the strait, which normally carries about a fifth of global oil. The US has responded with a naval blockade of Iranian ports and has escorted tankers through the waterway, while the US military says all mines have been cleared. The incident adds to fears of disruption to a key oil chokepoint.

stories.headline: Archaeologists hunt for Roman emperor statue missing in Scotland
stories.claim: Archaeologists will search Scotland for missing parts of a Roman bronze statue after finding the leg may have been erected locally.
stories.summary: Archaeologists are preparing to search Scotland for the missing parts of a gilded bronze statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius after new analysis suggested the leg was not looted from England. The lower leg was found in a bog at Milsington in the Scottish Borders in 1820 and was long assumed to have been plundered from a southern site such as York. Close examination now suggests it was carefully dismantled at the end of its life, pointing to a Roman decommissioning near the frontier. National Museums Scotland curators say forts near the find spot may hold clues. A replica statue incorporating the leg goes on display at the National Museum of Scotland in Edinburgh from Saturday, in the Roman Scotland exhibition running until 18 April.

stories.headline: Most large firms plan higher open-weight AI use to cap bills, study shows

stories.headline: Some under-25s should get fewer benefits, Milburn review to say
stories.claim: Alan Milburn's welfare review, due Tuesday, is expected to cut some benefits for under-25s and push £bn into youth employment support.
stories.summary: Some young people in Britain could see their benefits cut under a radical overhaul of the welfare system expected from a government-commissioned review by Alan Milburn. The report, due to be published on Tuesday after a year of work, is expected to move under-25s off the health element of universal credit and the personal independence payment (Pip), placing them on the basic universal credit rate instead. Milburn said the plans would not be pain-free and would affect both existing and new claimants, while the exact amounts will not be clear until legislation early next year. The review is aimed at the roughly one million young people in the UK who are not in education, employment or training (Neets), and it would also fund more job support. Labour MPs are already uneasy, and savings to the Treasury could take almost a decade to materialise.
key_points: Alan Milburn's year-long review is due to be published on Tuesday and is expected to recommend moving under-25s off the health element of universal credit and Pip.

Under-25s would instead receive the basic universal credit rate, with some eligible for a new additional cost allowance; those with severe disabilities who cannot work would get a higher-rate benefit.
About 430,000 of the four million people claiming Pip in England and Wales are aged 16 to 24.
Milburn proposes billions of pounds for youth employment support, including work placements, job subsidies and personal advisers, with sanctions for those who do not engage.
Just under one million young people in the UK are Neets, a rise of 3% year on year, according to ONS data for April to June.

stories.headline: A new camera technology could dramatically improve how smartphones take photos at night
stories.claim: Metalenz has acquired PxE Holographic Imaging, whose HoloCoder tech could boost smartphone low-light capture, but it is not yet in any phone.
stories.summary: A Boston company, Metalenz, has bought PxE Holographic Imaging, the developer of HoloCoder, a technology that could make smartphone cameras far better at night. Instead of a standard colour filter that blocks roughly 60% of incoming light, HoloCoder uses a microscopic optical layer to bend different wavelengths toward the correct pixels, and PxE claims sensors can collect up to 2.5 times more light without getting bigger. The same sensor could also capture depth information, potentially removing the need for separate depth-sensing hardware. Metalenz is also eyeing robotics and autonomous vehicles. However, the technology has not yet been shown in a commercial phone, and no manufacturer has confirmed plans to use it. Metalenz expects consumer electronics adoption by late 2027 or early 2028, so this is a longer-term development for phone buyers.

stories.claim: Greenpeace has logged over 500 oil spills since the US-Iran war began, covering about 20,000 sq km, threatening Gulf ecosystems.
stories.summary: Oil slicks covering an estimated 20,000 square kilometres, roughly the size of Wales, have spread across the Gulf since the US war with Iran began on 28 February. Greenpeace has identified more than 500 spills through satellite monitoring, and October was the worst month with more than 30 attacks on tankers in and around the Strait of Hormuz. Scientists warn that oil coating mangroves and birds, combined with shallow warm waters, could cause lasting damage to corals, fish and turtle habitats. Gulf states have launched clean-ups in some cases, but researchers in Iran and the Gulf say they have been told not to speak publicly. The Strait of Hormuz is one of the world's busiest oil shipping routes, so the attacks also bear on global oil supply and prices.
key_points: Greenpeace has identified more than 500 oil spills linked to the war since 28 February.
Cumulative slicks total roughly 20,000 square kilometres, according to Greenpeace's satellite mapping.
More than 133 attacks on oil tankers have occurred since the conflict began, with over 30 in October alone.
Shorelines and protected areas, including Shidvar Island and the Musandam national park, have been affected.
The UAE closed beaches and launched a clean-up after the Gem No 2 spill, which was reported stopped on 30 October.
Researchers say full damage cannot be assessed because on-the-ground access is severely restricted.

stories.headline: What to know about this year’s UN climate talks
stories.claim: COP31 UN climate talks are under way in Antalya, Turkey, with the US absent and fossil fuels and climate finance in focus.
stories.summary: The UN climate summit COP31 opened on 8 November in Antalya, Turkey, and is due to close on 20 November, with Turkey and Australia as cohosts. The talks come against a tense backdrop: the war in Iran has pushed energy prices up, and the US, which has withdrawn from the Paris Agreement, sends no formal delegation. The UN Environment Programme has warned that warming is likely to pass 1.5C within a few years. Negotiators face the question of how to fund cuts and adaptation, with rich nations giving $136.7 billion in 2024 against a goal of $300 billion a year by 2035. Fossil fuels are another flashpoint, since the 2025 deal did not mention them once.

Turkey and Australia are cohosting, and both face criticism over their fossil fuel links.

A proposed pledge would raise electricity's share of global energy use to 35% by 2035.

Because inflation is rising, the Bank of England raised rates to 4% last week, and analysts now see a further rise in December as a live possibility.

stories.headline: Spanish protesters hurl fireworks at police during mass strike
stories.claim: Spain's first general strike in 14 years over housing turned violent in several cities, with 53 arrests and disputed turnout figures.
stories.summary: Spain's first general strike since 2012 brought hundreds of thousands onto the streets to protest the housing affordability crisis, and it turned violent in several cities. Masked protesters threw fireworks at police and smashed shop windows in Barcelona, while riot police in Madrid used tear gas and batons, and at least 53 people were arrested. Unions put participation at 60 per cent of workers and said 4 million took part, while employers' groups put it at about 3 per cent. The strike comes less than three weeks before a snap general election on 29 November, in which Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's Socialists trail the conservative People's Party. The government's housing reforms were rejected by parliament last month, and the protests were fuelled by the eviction and death of an 87-year-old Madrid woman.

stories.headline: Strategy, the World’s Biggest Corporate Bitcoin Holder, to Be Dropped From MSCI Indexes
stories.claim: MSCI confirms it will drop Strategy (MSTR) from its MSCI USA, World and ACWI indexes at the close on 30 November 2026.
stories.summary: Strategy, the world's largest corporate bitcoin holder, will be removed from MSCI's flagship equity indexes after the close on Monday, 30 November 2026. JPMorgan estimates up to $2.8 billion of Strategy shares could be sold by index funds if MSCI removal happens, with a further $8.8 billion at risk if other major indexes follow. Strategy argues the impact will be limited, as MSCI-tracking funds hold only about 3.1% of its basic shares. The same review adds Moderna and Aritzia to the MSCI World, with 100 deletions across the ACWI.

stories.headline: Quebec’s strategic maple-syrup reserve is running dry
stories.claim: Quebec's strategic maple syrup reserve is nearly empty and expected to be fully depleted by end of February.
stories.summary: Quebec's world-first strategic maple syrup reserve is set to be completely depleted by the end of February, according to the producers' body PPAQ. The reserve, spread across three warehouses and able to hold about 60 million kilograms, was created in 2000 to stabilise prices and supply. Its stock stood at about 18 million kilograms in February, and the PPAQ says strong demand, especially from the United States, has been drawing it down. Quebec produces about 90% of Canada's maple syrup and over 70% of the world's supply. The $1.2 billion industry relies on weather for sap flow, so a bad harvest would leave the market with little buffer. The PPAQ says the reserve needs replenishing and the sector must expand to meet demand. Canadian maple exports are rising, while the reserve's depletion reflects processors buying up stock rather than a shortage at the farm level.
key_points: Quebec's PPAQ says the strategic maple syrup reserve will be completely depleted by the end of February.

stories.market_take: A niche commodity story with negligible effect on listed markets.

stories.headline: UK fraudster who invented ‘too good to be true’ takeover bid given suspended sentence
stories.claim: UK fraudster who faked a £154m takeover bid for Touchstone Exploration gets two-year suspended sentence.
stories.summary: A British man who invented a fake £154 million takeover bid for Touchstone Exploration has been spared jail. Christopher Woolcott, 44, used ChatGPT to create false bank, law firm and private equity documents, and met the chief executive in person while posing as an American buyer's agent. He had bought shares in the Canadian oil and gas company, which is listed in London, and stood to make about £70,000 if the fake deal had leaked. Southwark Crown Court heard that Touchstone's executives quickly spotted the papers as amateurish. Judge Usha Karu handed him a two-year sentence, suspended for two years, plus 200 hours of community service and £4,627 in costs. The case highlights how easily fabricated deal rumours can be spread on social platforms, and it is a reminder of the market-abuse risks around small-cap takeover speculation.

stories.headline: Vodafone cuts 3,000 roles, plans 2,300 more in Germany and takes $5.4 billion hit as Africa becomes the British telecom giant’s growth engine
stories.claim: Vodafone posted a €3.6bn half-year loss from a German writedown, cut jobs, and raised its full-year forecast on African growth.

Chief executive Margherita Della Valle is cutting around 3,000 roles across Europe and shared operations, with another 2,300 planned in Germany, bringing the total to roughly 5,300. stories.headline: EU household electricity and gas prices fell in the first half of 2026: Who pays the most?

The technology, Mext, was acquired from a company of the same name in June and uses machine learning models running on a single CPU core to move memory pages between DRAM and cheaper NVMe flash before applications need them. AMD says the software could cut enterprise server costs by up to 83 percent and that 145 systems already run it, saving customers about $5 million in DRAM costs. The Register notes that tests show performance falling to 80 percent with only a quarter of memory in DRAM, and that virtualised environments need one core per VM. The software will be exclusive to AMD hardware and sold as a licence through OEM partners, as memory remains tight in AI data centres.
key_points: AMD acquired the Mext memory-offload technology in June and says it can keep up to 99 percent of performance with half the DRAM.
The system uses AI models on a CPU core to predict and preload memory pages from flash storage into DRAM.
AMD claims server cost savings of up to 83 percent, with 145 systems deployed and about $5 million in avoided DRAM costs.
Tests cited show 95 percent performance with half the memory in DRAM on an EDA suite, and 80 percent with only 25 percent DRAM.
The software is licensed through OEM partners and is exclusive to AMD hardware; virtualised setups need one core per VM.
The Register notes performance penalties exist, so AMD's claims of no impact are overstated.
stories.market_take: A modest positive for AMD's enterprise server business, though the effect on revenue is unclear.

stories.headline: Vercel data reveals AI models now have a half-life of just six weeks
stories.claim: Vercel data suggests AI models have a half-life of about six weeks, with teams switching quickly to newer models.
stories.summary: Developers are abandoning AI models faster than ever, according to Vercel's AI Gateway report for November 2026, which estimates a model's usage halves in about six weeks. Teams using paid services stick with a new model for an average of four weeks before switching. Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5, launched on 22 September 2026, was the top model by spend in its first full month and drew just over 14 percent of October spending. Anthropic models dominate the most-used list, with Sonnet 5.5 at 26 percent and Haiku 5.5 at 22 percent. Video models are also spreading, with one in six AI development teams using one, up from 10 percent. The findings come from Vercel's own gateway transactions, so they reflect its customer base rather than the whole market.
key_points: Vercel estimates AI models have an effective half-life of around six weeks, as teams switch to newer releases.
Teams using paid AI services stay with a new model for about four weeks on average.
Claude Opus 5.5, launched 22 September 2026, was the top model by spend in October at just over 14 percent.
Sonnet 5.5 (26 percent), Haiku 5.5 (22 percent) and Haiku 4.5 (20 percent) are the most widely used paid models, all from Anthropic.
By September, almost 17 percent of usage was on models less than two weeks old, showing early adoption is rising.
One in six AI development teams now use a video model, up from 10 percent; OpenAI's GPT-Image-2.5 led image generation spend.

stories.summary: Microsoft will switch on Anthropic's Claude models by default for UK Copilot customers from 9 December, according to The Register. stories.headline: Anduril says its first satellite can see adversaries maneuver in orbital night
stories.claim: Anduril says its first satellite, Anduril-216, has demonstrated an infrared sensor that tracks spacecraft during orbital night.
stories.summary: Anduril Industries says its oven-sized demonstration satellite, Anduril-216, can track other spacecraft in Earth's shadow using a long-wave infrared sensor. The satellite launched on a SpaceX rideshare in July and flies about 590 km above Earth, spending roughly a third of each orbit in darkness. It addresses a gap in optical tracking, since space traffic monitors can lose satellites that manoeuvre during eclipse. Anduril said it was funded from its own capital and that the platform was built by Apex Space. The company is focusing on space domain awareness data for the US military and says it is not yet selling the system as a merchant supplier.

The sensor detects heat signatures, letting it track objects during orbital night.

stories.headline: Shipping giant Maersk probes 'IT security incident,' data theft

stories.headline: Google gooses Python AI performance by... removing Python
stories.claim: Google has open-sourced XSE, a C++ serving engine that replaces Python in production ML inference.
stories.summary: Google has open-sourced XSE, the XLA Serving Engine, a system that runs machine-learning models without a Python interpreter in the serving path. It already handles more than six million queries per second across services including Search, Google Ads and YouTube Shorts. In Google's tests on short requests, XSE delivered two to five times the throughput of its best optimised Python server while using a quarter of the memory. The tool targets smaller, task-specific models such as ranking and recommendation rather than large language models, which are better served by vLLM or SGLang. It compiles computations via OpenXLA and works best on Google's TPUs, though it also runs on GPUs and CPUs.
key_points: Google has open-sourced XSE, the XLA Serving Engine, which removes Python from the serving pipeline.
XSE already handles over six million queries per second across Search, Ads and YouTube Shorts.

It is aimed at ranking, recommendation, embedding and vision models rather than large language models.
Models are exported in StableHLO and run on TPUs, GPUs or CPUs, with TorchTPU integration planned.
stories.market_take: Mildly positive for Google's TPU ecosystem; limited near-term market effect.

stories.headline: Facial recognition errors put ethnic minorities at risk of wrongful arrest, police watchdog warns
stories.claim: UK police inspectors warn that retrospective facial recognition errors and biases risk wrongful arrests of ethnic minorities.
stories.summary: A report from His Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary (HMICFRS), published on Wednesday, warns that British police could wrongly arrest innocent people if they treat retrospective facial recognition matches as evidence rather than leads. Inspectors found some investigators did not carry out enough checks before acting on potential matches, and in a few cases officers relied too heavily on the results. The report flags continuing bias in the algorithm, which is more likely to wrongly flag people from ethnic minorities, and says some custody images that should have been deleted were kept. It also notes there is no comprehensive legal framework for the technology. Campaigners such as Big Brother Watch called the findings alarming, while the National Police Chiefs' Council said it remains committed to responsible use.

stories.headline: United Airlines is grounding AI travel agents, and safety is just one of the concerns
stories.claim: United Airlines is blocking unauthorised third-party AI assistants from completing flight bookings for customers.
stories.summary: United Airlines has begun blocking unauthorised third-party AI assistants from booking flights on behalf of customers, a move that sets it apart from rivals that are opening up to AI agents. The airline says such tools could expose personal data, make unintended purchases, modify bookings or spend MileagePlus rewards without customers noticing. It also argues that certain safety steps, such as passengers confirming their checked bags contain no prohibited items, need direct acknowledgement and could clash with FAA and DOT rules. The policy covers United's own digital channels, travel agencies and flight aggregators, though AI assistants can still show United fares and options. CEO Scott Kirby told the Wall Street Journal he does not want to create another middleman. Amazon and several large banks have also restricted AI agents, while Delta reportedly allows authenticated assistants to book, showing the industry is split.

stories.headline: Fewer hours and higher wages – or more burnout and surveillance: employers told to prepare for AI
stories.claim: Australia's government has issued a best-practice guide on AI in the workplace, warning of job and surveillance risks.
stories.summary: Australia's workplace relations minister Amanda Rishworth has launched a best-practice guide on adopting AI at work, warning employers that the technology could bring either shorter hours and higher wages or more burnout and surveillance. The guide says entry-level jobs will be the first to be automated and that younger, older, First Nations, female and disabled workers face disproportionate impacts. The launch follows job cuts at Qantas (850 roles), National Australian Bank (2,500) and Canva (1,200), which are linked to AI and restructuring. The Reserve Bank of Australia has seen only tentative signs of AI affecting roles such as clerks, programmers and call-centre staff. Greens leader David Shoebridge argued the guidance is too weak and should be written into law. The government's stance is voluntary guidance rather than binding rules.

stories.headline: AWS distills its cloud into a local emulator that runs on your PC
stories.claim: AWS has released a free local emulator that serves its APIs on a developer's PC for testing without calling the cloud.
stories.summary: Amazon Web Services has released an AWS Emulator that runs locally on a laptop or development server and serves AWS API endpoints, letting developers test software without calling the real cloud. The tool is written in Rust, which AWS says keeps its CPU and memory use light, and it is free for tests that never touch AWS. It covers only services with API models in AWS's public repository, and it does not replicate everything, such as IAM policy evaluation or cross-account and cross-region behaviour. AWS publishes fidelity scores showing how closely each service matches the real cloud, and it offers an aws-emulator skill for AI coding agents to check whether a project will work. The release is a developer-tools move that lowers the barrier to building for AWS, and it is aimed at pulling more usage onto the cloud over time.

stories.headline: A third of UK businesses on Google Maps have no working website — and many of those that do are struggling to keep them up to date
stories.claim: A census finds a third of UK businesses with claimed Google listings have no working website, with health and beauty worst affected.
stories.summary: Roughly a third of UK businesses with a claimed Google Business Profile send customers to a page they do not control, such as a social profile, a booking app or a dead site. stories.headline: Disgraced former CA eMudhra blames buggy script for hopelessly weak certificates
stories.claim: eMudhra blames a buggy Python script for issuing weak digital certificates and is quitting the SSL/TLS certificate business.
stories.summary: Indian certificate authority eMudhra says a buggy Python script caused it to issue digital certificates with dangerously weak keys. The keys, meant to be 48 bytes, were truncated to a single byte, making them recoverable from public information. The error stemmed from a key-generation ceremony on 30 April 2025, when hardware security modules were unavailable because of supply constraints. A Mozilla team member spotted the flaw, browser makers stopped trusting eMudhra's certificates, and the firm has now exited the SSL/TLS business. The company says it will make improvements following an independent review.
key_points: eMudhra says the key-generation script truncated private keys, leaving them far weaker than intended.

stories.summary: The SS United States, a former transatlantic liner once the fastest in the world, was intentionally sunk off Destin, Florida, on Wednesday to become the world's largest artificial ocean reef. stories.summary: New York's Attorney General Letitia James found that T-Mobile was not complying with the state's Affordable Broadband Act, which requires low-cost home internet for eligible low-income households. T-Mobile had applied monthly data caps to its plans, throttling speeds to as low as 650 kilobits per second after 50GB of use, which the state said could happen in about four days of typical use. The company also offered the plans only where it had 5G wireless deployed and blocked search engines from indexing details. Under an agreement, T-Mobile will remove the caps, extend the plans to all places in New York where it offers home internet, and let search engines index the plan details. T-Mobile said it would keep the same low price while updating the plan.

stories.summary: Google DeepMind has unveiled AlphaProof Code, an AI system that uses mathematical proofs to show that software meets its security specifications. In a demonstration on Signal's encryption protocol, the team says the work took four weeks, where such work typically takes years. Earlier verification efforts had stopped at the design stage, whereas this one checked the actual cryptographic code running on users' devices. Experts defined the security requirements, and AI agents built on Gemini Carbon wrote more than six million lines in the Lean proof language, with about one percent flagged for human review. Two deliberately planted bugs were caught. Signal's CTO said the approach strengthens trust in privacy, and DeepMind plans to extend the method to power grids and medical devices.
key_points: DeepMind unveiled AlphaProof Code, which mathematically proves software meets security specifications.
It was demonstrated on the cryptographic core of Signal's encryption protocol.
The work took four weeks, compared with the years such efforts typically take.
AI agents wrote over six million lines in Lean, with about 1 percent flagged for human review.
Two deliberately planted bugs were caught immediately.
DeepMind plans to apply the method to power grids and medical devices.

stocks.reason: Showcases DeepMind's AI capabilities in formal verification, a modest boost to its AI credentials.

stories.headline: NASA asks Earthlings to wave as Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away
stories.claim: NASA invites the public to flash the letters VGR in Morse code on November 17 as Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth.
stories.summary: NASA says Voyager 1 will become the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth, a distance of about 25.9 billion kilometres, on 18 November at 10:16 UTC. The spacecraft is travelling at roughly 61,000 kph. NASA is inviting people to flash the mission's designation VGR in Morse code after sunset on 17 November as a symbolic gesture, though Voyager 1's cameras were switched off decades ago so it cannot see them. The article notes the probe suffered a communications hiccup last month and that its sibling, Voyager 2, will reach the same milestone about nine years later, with its communication uncertain given dwindling power.

stories.headline: Apple on Fatal Vehicle Crash Near Apple Park: 'Our Hearts Are Broken'
stories.claim: Apple responded after an Apple employee was charged over a fatal crash near Apple Park that killed a two-year-old girl.
stories.summary: Apple has said its hearts are broken after a fatal crash near the Apple Park Visitor Center in Cupertino, California. According to the Santa Clara County Sheriff's Office, an Apple employee, Eric Chen Su, was arrested and charged with gross vehicular manslaughter after a collision on a Friday last week. Authorities say he was reportedly driving 90 to 100 miles per hour when he struck the back of a stopped car carrying a two-year-old girl and an adult babysitter. The child died in hospital, while the babysitter was seriously injured and Su had minor injuries. His charges have reportedly been upgraded to murder and assault with a deadly weapon. Apple did not say whether he has been fired or placed on leave, and the case is now before the court.

stories.headline: Police to crack down on 500 most prolific shoplifters
stories.claim: UK police will target 500 prolific shoplifters with city centre bans and GPS tags in a 16-force trial scheme.
stories.summary: Police in England and Wales will use criminal behaviour orders against around 500 of the most prolific shoplifters, in a trial involving 16 forces including the Metropolitan Police. The orders can ban offenders from specific city centre areas, impose electronic tags, curfews and addiction treatment, and carry up to five years in jail for breaches. Research cited by the government says 10 per cent of shoplifters cause 70 per cent of store thefts, and the British Retail Consortium estimates about 5.5m thefts a year costing retailers £2.2bn. An initial £2.5m is being made available to the forces. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood framed the plan as part of a government push to cut shop theft, which retail chiefs call a national emergency.

stories.headline: Amnesty says UN, South Sudan officials failed to prevent village massacre
stories.claim: Amnesty says UN and South Sudan authorities failed to act on warnings before a March massacre that killed over 200 people.
stories.summary: Amnesty International's new report says UN peacekeepers (UNMISS) and South Sudanese authorities failed to act on clear warnings before an armed attack on Abiemnom village on 1 March that killed more than 200 people. Amnesty says between 1,000 and 1,500 armed men from Mayom County carried out the attack, and satellite images show more than 230 structures burned. UNMISS says it had asked the national army for reinforcements and sheltered about 2,500 people, and sent 40 more police after the attack. Amnesty has called for an independent investigation, as South Sudan prepares for elections on 22 December, which some fear could undermine a fragile 2018 peace deal.

stories.summary: A Vogue article reports on eBay's latest Watchlist report, published 10 November 2026, which examines how new creative directors are lifting secondhand demand for luxury fashion. Searches for Matthieu Blazy rose 291% after his first Chanel collection, while Demna searches rose 42% after his first Gucci show. Jonathan Anderson's Dior debut lifted searches for him by 92%, and John Galliano-era Dior average sale prices rose 81%. Celebrity sightings are cited as a key driver of price rises, for example The Row's Margaux Bag, up 137% year-on-year. The report suggests that consumers are increasingly turning to resale to buy into current trends at better value, which brands may need to watch closely.
key_points: eBay's Fall/Winter 2026 Watchlist report, published 10 November 2026, tracks resale trends linked to creative director changes.
Searches for Matthieu Blazy jumped 291% after his first Chanel collection, and Chanel listings from the Karl Lagerfeld era rose 87%.
Demna's first Gucci show lifted searches for him by 42%, and Tom Ford-era Gucci listings rose 49%.
Average sale prices for John Galliano-era Dior rose 81%, following Jonathan Anderson's first couture show at Dior.
Celebrity sightings are cited by eBay as a major driver of price rises, with The Row's Margaux Bag up 137%.
Chanel moved from fifth place in 2025 to third among eBay's top-purchased luxury brands in 2026.
stories.market_take: Strong secondhand demand for past archives may be a useful signal for luxury groups, though the effect on listed shares is likely small.

stories.headline: Vacheron Constantin Just Gave Its Retro-Inspired Fiftysix Watches a Modern Makeover
stories.claim: Vacheron Constantin unveils two refreshed Fiftysix watches with 1950s-inspired modern design.
stories.summary: Swiss maison Vacheron Constantin has unveiled two new Fiftysix watches, the collection launched in 2018 and named after the 1956 Ref. 6073 dress watch. stories.headline: Lara Saget’s Sculptures Mine the Ancient, Alchemical, and Divine
stories.claim: Sculptor Lara Saget opens her first New York solo show, exploring spirituality, geology and regeneration.
stories.summary: Brooklyn-based sculptor Lara Saget has opened her first New York City solo exhibition, "and the world came apart", at Trotter&Sholer on Elizabeth Street, curated by Sarah Darro. The show opened on 7 November and runs until 19 December. It includes copper-alloy and granite wall works inspired by early cave drawings and glass sculptures of the ancient Judean date palm and the Joshua tree. Saget recently received a master's in divinity and became an ordained minister, and her spirituality informs the work. She uses a lost-wax casting process that dates back around 6,000 years, which she carries out by hand with a team in India.
